statement: One record per audit finding. A finding may honestly be open, unreviewed or accepted, but it may not be absent, and it may not carry a disposition without evidence. Status describes what is known about the defect; disposition describes what has been done about it. Neither implies the other. Each finding also names the deduplicated root cause it belongs to, so the register and the audit's remediation order use one vocabulary. A finding the taxonomy does not cover says so, rather than being filed under an approximate neighbour.

marRootCauses.title: Cross-tenant resource authorization is not parent-bound everywhere
Studio materializer has no universal creator-ownership safety boundary
No single clean canonical product acceptance run exists
Generation has no durable project-scoped single-flight and idempotent start identity
State transitions have no unified durable CAS/version authority
Process-local PostgreSQL cache is not multi-instance coherent
Project deletion is not a data-erasure lifecycle
AI memory has no correct tenant/project isolation boundary
Generated Lua security evidence is not a blocking production gate
No authoritative Luau compile/type and generated-code policy gate
Untrusted AI input has no complete instruction/data security boundary
Runtime gameplay acceptance is missing as a machine-measured capability
Spatial and multiplayer invariants are not runtime-proven
World ownership still has an unfinished canonical transition
Runtime release-pair authority can drift
Chaos and recovery are not tested on real failure boundaries
Backup, restore and PITR are not a production capability
Execution-level and tenant-level FinOps control plane is missing
Privacy lifecycle is incomplete
Raw user content can enter logs without central redaction
Observability has no common end-to-end identity envelope
Incident-response control plane is undefined
Frontend main governance does not protect CI authority
Supply-chain release authority is not immutable end-to-end
Database operational governance is incomplete
Global storage write serialization and fairness are not capacity-proven
Production performance envelope is unknown
Browser lifecycle compatibility is not cross-engine proven
WCAG 2.2 AA is not an acceptance gate
Supply-chain compliance and provenance are incomplete
GitHub governance has further unclosed controls
Architecture has ownership abstractions without a complete authority map
Fuzz and property testing are systematically missing
Mutation testing is not a general quality gate
CSRF protection is not formally closed
Dead and legacy code, and naming drift
Policy and documentation cleanup

findings.title: Generation accepted a blueprint id belonging to another project
findings.notes: Authorized the URL projectId but resolved a body-supplied blueprintId. Reproduced against the baseline: the cross-project request answered 200 and a pipeline started for the other project's blueprint. Fixed at both the route and the service boundary.

findings.title: Generation start wrote project, execution and history as three independent durable writes
findings.notes: A rejection after the first write left a project falsely generating with an incremented count and no execution able to repair it. Fixed by committing all three in one applyDurableBatch, mirroring GenerationOutcomeCoordinator.

findings.title: Execution identity derived from Date.now collided within a millisecond
findings.notes: generation_executions is keyed by execution id alone across every project and recordExecution writes through a blind upsert, so a collision destroyed the other project's execution. Reproduced: two starts left one record instead of two.

findings.title: Security exception expiry validated against a frozen audit date
findings.notes: The validate:security-scanners policy compares expiry against a hardcoded 2026-08-01, so exceptions that expired on 2026-08-15 still pass on this baseline. The fix injects a real UTC clock and turns the gate red until the exceptions are renewed or removed.

findings.title: No suppression of a second concurrent generation for the same project
findings.notes: The project lock covers only the short start critical section. Two starts legitimately produce two executions and two generation-count increments. Deliberately left out of the start-atomicity slice.

findings.title: An older overlapping run can overwrite a newer run's terminal project state
findings.notes: Nothing restricts terminal project updates to the current execution. Depends on AUDIT-DUP-GENERATION-001 for its main trigger.

findings.title: Canonical generation is not resumed or reconciled after restart
findings.notes: The execution record is durable but the worker queue is process-local, so a restart leaves executions durably running with no owner. AutonomousOrchestrator already implements persisted sessions, recovery claims and idempotent recovery and is the pattern to reuse.

findings.title: Shutdown does not drain the canonical generation queue
findings.notes: Same root as AUDIT-RECOVERY-001. SIGTERM can end the process mid-generation and leave a durable running execution.

findings.title: The mature generation queue has no production consumer at all
findings.notes: Found while mapping runtime ownership. GenerationQueue offers status tracking, priority and retry counters, but its only importer is its own barrel and nothing imports that barrel; its only other reference is a test. Canonical generation uses a serial in-memory queue with an effective concurrency of one, so one long run blocks every other generation.

findings.title: An unreferenced legacy generation pipeline cluster remains in the tree
findings.notes: GenerationPipeline.ts has zero production importers, and GenerationRegistry.ts, GenerationManifest.ts and GenerationReport.ts are imported only by it, so the cluster is reachable from nothing. GenerationBlueprint.ts in the same directory has 13 importers and is a shared contract that must not be removed with the island.

findings.title: Realtime reports a pipeline completed before artifact and validation stages run
findings.notes: An agent DAG completing is not canonical generation completing. If the artifact stage then fails, realtime says completed while the durable execution says failed.

findings.title: Terminal failure records lose pipeline_steps recorded before the failure
findings.notes: After an artifact recorder failure the terminal execution is written without complete steps, so a refreshed client sees zero completed, zero failed and zero known even though agents ran.

findings.title: Evaluation, memory and planning events broadcast to every connected socket
findings.notes: Thirteen emissions sit in the same switch as the project-room emitter with the same project identifier in scope and broadcast past it anyway. Client-side filtering is not a security boundary: the unauthorized socket already received the payload. Now tracked as global-bypassing-available-scope in the matrix broadcasts section.

findings.title: Execution traces broadcast globally from a listener with no project context
findings.notes: Payload carries executionId, nodeId, agentId, evaluationScore and error. Distinct remediation from SEC-REALTIME-GLOBAL-001: the tracer listener receives no project, so scoping requires plumbing context in first. Tracked as global-no-project-context.

findings.title: Pipeline events fall back to a global broadcast when no project is known
findings.notes: emitForProject addresses the project room when evt.projectId is present and broadcasts to everyone when it is not. The fallback should fail closed rather than widen the audience.

findings.title: Cross-tenant denial is essentially unevidenced across the API
findings.notes: Of 206 operations, five have a test that issues a real foreign request, fifteen have evidence that only asserts strings in handler source, and 186 have none recorded. The existing negativeEvidence column mostly proves missing authentication, which is a weaker property than cross-owner denial. One family, body-blueprint-project, now has a behavioural harness on integration/wave-0 (a5ca5fe3); the rest of the inventory is still unevidenced, so this stays open. Closed as a count and reopened as a list. The matrix now carries mar001Category, which separates the question the count was conflating: 91 operations have no per-resource authorization to make, 53 authorize the very identifier they act on so the mismatch cannot be written, 51 have a verified mechanism, and 15 are real gaps. Those 15 are the whole of the remaining MAR-001 debt and are enumerated in SEC-MAR001-REMAINING-GAPS-001.

findings.title: Ninety-eight operations still have no object-binding verdict
findings.notes: This pass reviewed the concept pipeline and artifact families, the game-generation blueprint reads and the body-blueprint family. Operator and global-runtime endpoints were deliberately excluded by scope decision. Everything else is recorded as indirect-unreviewed, which is a gap and not a safety claim.

findings.title: Eight operations authorize against an identifier inside a caller-supplied body object
findings.notes: economy, world, simulation, lifecycle and generation-v2 take the whole blueprint from req.body and pass blueprint.id to requireProjectAccess, using a field named like a blueprint identifier as a project identifier. There is no cross-tenant escape today because the identifier must resolve to a reachable project, but nothing binds the payload to stored state, and the naming confusion becomes a real hole if the two identifier spaces ever overlap. lifecycle POST /tick is the one variant that first asserts blueprint.id equals gameId.

findings.title: Artifact review attribution is taken from the request body
findings.notes: approve, reject and comment record reviewedBy from req.body with a fallback to the literal user, rather than from the authenticated session, so approval evidence is caller-asserted. Authorization itself is sound: router.param resolves the artifact to its project and conceals denial as 404.

findings.title: Room membership on project switch is not proven to be exclusive
findings.notes: Leaving the previous project room is not clearly guaranteed when a socket moves between projects, so a socket may remain in several rooms.

findings.title: Editing a project does not update its existing blueprint
findings.notes: Create, generate, edit the brief, generate again can reuse the old blueprint. Generation also references a mutable blueprint rather than an immutable versioned snapshot, which weakens reproducibility, forensic traceability and rollback.

findings.title: Design chat does not change the canonical blueprint
findings.notes: Chat persists the conversation but a design change agreed in chat is not a blueprint change, so the assistant can state that the design was updated while the next generation still uses the old blueprint.

findings.title: Structured Lua generation output is not reliably parseable
findings.notes: Two canonical end-to-end runs failed to produce a package. Native structured output, token budgets and constrained repair were addressed on other branches; whole-response repair remains the main truncation risk.

findings.title: Explicit user intent is not authoritative across agents
findings.notes: Frontend project creation defaults genre and game type, the backend stores those defaults as explicit metadata, and downstream agents treat the random design seed with more authority than the stated requirement. The result is a coherent but different game. Requirements now carry identity where they are produced and each run records which of them it can show evidence for (2edb5d68). The chain does not yet carry identifiers past the requirements stage, so the recorded coverage is low by design and this stays open until downstream agents cite them.

findings.title: No cardinality gate between a stated requirement and the generated world
findings.notes: A requirement for exactly three objectives produced two. Validation is structural, syntactic and playability oriented; it does not assert that the system built what was asked for.

findings.title: Simulation is not a Roblox runtime
findings.notes: The limitation is real but it is now stated rather than hidden. The engine is registered as canonical for blueprint-simulation only, its responsibility says it is not a Roblox runtime, and PlaytestAgent explicitly records when no real runtime test occurred. What remains open is the absence of a runtime playtest capability, tracked as STUDIO-PLAY-ACCEPTANCE-001.

findings.title: Autonomous lifecycle stays fail-closed without server-owned evidence
findings.notes: Remaining in CREATED without evidence is the correct behaviour. It also demonstrates that the lifecycle is not yet a working end-to-end capability, which is a roadmap fact rather than a defect.

findings.title: Project-scoped artifact store ownership and commit marker semantics
findings.notes: Requires project ownership, writes the commit marker last, checks project, pipeline, stage and hash, and requires both a world model and Lua before a generation package is valid.

findings.title: Autonomous orchestrator implements real restart recovery
findings.notes: Persisted sessions, readiness, interruption marking, recovery claims and idempotent recovery. This is the pattern canonical generation should reuse for AUDIT-RECOVERY-001.

findings.title: The production contract test accepts a failed generation
findings.notes: The contract allows canonical generation to end completed or failed and continues, and the Studio portion asserts a disconnected response rather than package, transfer, import and play. Green CI therefore does not imply a working product vertical.

findings.title: The restart test proves durability, not recovery
findings.notes: It asserts that the execution record still exists after restart. It does not require a running execution to be resumed or reconciled to a terminal state, so it passes with a permanently orphaned execution. A reconciliation test now proves the workflow is closed rather than merely persisted (186d1a08), but the original weak restart test is unchanged, so this stays open.

findings.title: The production contract runs against in-memory storage
findings.notes: A contract named production that sets the storage provider to in-memory is not a production-equivalent persistence test.

findings.title: Validator and generator scripts are outside the typecheck boundary
findings.marNote: No MAR root cause covers build and typecheck coverage of tooling.
findings.notes: The typecheck script covers server/tsconfig.json only, so the scripts that enforce the control gates are checked by eslint and by running them, but never type-checked. Found while extending the authorization matrix generator.

findings.title: A release can start healthy without a real AI provider
findings.notes: The checked-in production configuration does not require a provider, so the backend can start in a deterministic fallback and still present itself as healthy without its main capability.

findings.title: Health is liveness rather than readiness
findings.marNote: No MAR root cause covers service health and readiness semantics. MAR-021 is observability identity, which is a different concern.
findings.notes: It does not sufficiently verify durable storage state, provider availability or generation capability.

findings.title: Provider logging can write prompts and generated code to backend logs
findings.notes: User briefs, prompts, AI context and generated Lua reaching logs is a privacy, intellectual property and retention problem. Fixed by shape rather than by discipline: the telemetry helper takes measurements, not payloads, and payload previews are bounded and unavailable in production whatever the flag says.

findings.title: Generation does not enforce tier limits before starting
findings.notes: Combined with duplicate generation, long provider calls and a single serial queue, this allows resource amplification and denial of wallet.

findings.title: Profile email can diverge from the password credential key
findings.marNote: The MAR taxonomy has no auth credential lifecycle root cause. The nearest neighbours are MAR-019 privacy lifecycle and MAR-022 incident response, and neither covers verified email identity.
findings.notes: The credential is looked up by normalized email, so a profile change that does not atomically migrate the credential breaks password login.

findings.title: Password reset is not implemented behind an interface that claims it is
findings.marNote: Same taxonomy gap as AUTH-EMAIL-IDENTITY-001: no MAR root cause covers credential recovery as a product capability.
findings.notes: The endpoint accepts the request without token issuance, expiry, one-time semantics or credential replacement, while the interface can tell the user to check their inbox.

findings.title: Project version history is process-local
findings.marNote: No MAR root cause covers durable product state that is neither a tenancy nor a deletion concern. MAR-025 is database governance, which is a different claim.
findings.notes: Version history held in a process-local map is erased by restart, which is a severe mismatch for a system that generates autonomously and offers rollback.

findings.title: Preferences are documented as persisted but held in memory
findings.notes: Restart loses them.

findings.title: Actions and base images are pinned by tag rather than digest
findings.notes: Major version tags and floating image tags are a reproducibility and supply-chain hardening gap rather than an active vulnerability.

findings.title: The current backend CI failure set must be re-established before remediation
findings.notes: The audit history contains two different explanations of the same failure, stale project-ownership fixtures and a Studio runtime closed to exported transition. Neither may be treated as current until re-verified against the present head. Recorded so no remediation is planned against a stale failure.

findings.title: Repository visibility and branch protection must be established as fact
findings.notes: Both repositories were public during the audit and the effective rulesets could not be read unambiguously. If the code is intended to be proprietary this is a governance risk. Requires an authenticated check rather than inference.

findings.title: No end-to-end proof from generation to Roblox Play with runtime evidence
findings.notes: The required chain is fresh project, canonical generation, package, transfer, import, scene materialized, scripts placed, play, objective works, evidence captured. Until it exists the platform is not proven end to end.

findings.title: Dynamic assurance has not been performed
findings.notes: Penetration testing, AI red teaming, chaos and fault injection, load and soak testing, a real backup and restore drill with measured objectives, full accessibility review, browser compatibility, database index and migration review, and project deletion and privacy behaviour are all unperformed. Recorded as one open block so their absence is visible rather than implied.

findings.title: The user-self authorization test fails intermittently under parallel load
findings.marNote: Test-suite determinism is not a MAR root cause. It is recorded because a flaky test is evidence that cannot be relied on.
findings.notes: It passes in isolation and times out at about five seconds when the full security suite runs in parallel. Reproduced twice in this session, once on a clean baseline with all local changes removed, so it is a baseline flake rather than a regression. It matters more than an ordinary flake because it is one of only five operations in the matrix with real behavioural cross-tenant evidence, so when it flakes that evidence is unreliable.

findings.title: A generation run read the live blueprint rather than an immutable snapshot
findings.notes: An edit landing mid-run changed what the run was building. Each execution now binds to a versioned snapshot with a content hash, so what a run consumed stays recoverable after the fact.

findings.title: System defaults were presented downstream as user-stated intent
findings.notes: Fields the system filled in were indistinguishable from fields the user chose, so a generated game could satisfy a requirement nobody asked for. Assumed fields are now marked as such, and requirements derived from them are not reported as user-stated.

findings.title: Requirements carried no identity, so no run could show which ones it satisfied
findings.notes: Requirements reached downstream agents as opaque strings, so the only available answer about coverage was prose. Requirements now carry identifiers and a run reports which of them it can show evidence for. The measured number is deliberately low: the chain does not yet carry identifiers past the requirements stage, and that gap is now a recorded number rather than an assumption about it.

findings.title: Valid JSON was discarded when a model added prose after it
findings.notes: The bracket-scan fallback sliced from the first bracket to the end of the string, so any trailing explanation destroyed a perfectly good response and the run fell back to canned content. Extraction now scans to the matching close, tracking string literals because generated Luau is delivered inside JSON strings and is full of braces. A response truncated before its closing bracket returns null rather than parsing a fragment.

findings.title: Structures reached generation prompts as the literal text [object Object]
findings.notes: Five agents summarised structures with a name-or-item fallback. An item without a name stringified to a placeholder, so the model was told a mechanic or system existed and given nothing about it, including in the prompt that generates the Lua. Values are now described so the content survives when there is no name.

findings.title: Refusing another tenant's Studio command disclosed that it existed and what state it was in
findings.notes: The binding itself was present: a caller authorized for one Studio client could not acknowledge or report on a command belonging to a client in another project. The refusal was the leak. A command owned by another tenant answered 403 and carried that command's lifecycle status in the response body, while a command that did not exist answered 404, so the difference confirmed existence and state. Both now answer identically and carry nothing about the resource. The runtime still distinguishes client_mismatch internally, so the server keeps knowing the difference and stops telling the caller.

findings.title: Studio protocol messages were authorized against a project the caller chose, not the client they acted on
findings.notes: POST /protocol/message resolved the project to authorize by preferring payload.projectId, then dispatched handlers such as COMMAND_ACK and COMMAND_RESULT which act on payload.clientId. A caller could therefore present a project they legitimately owned for the access check and another tenant's client for the work. The runtime's own client-to-command check did not catch it, because both identifiers named the same foreign client consistently; it was the authorization that pointed elsewhere. Reproduced against the baseline: the intruder's request moved the victim's command from sent to acknowledged. The client's project now wins whenever a clientId is present, and a projectId that disagrees with it is refused rather than resolved in either direction.

findings.title: The command disclosure closed on the REST path was still reachable over the protocol transport
findings.notes: COMMAND_ACK and COMMAND_RESULT returned the refusal reason and the command's lifecycle status, which is what SEC-STUDIO-COMMAND-DISCLOSURE-001 removed from the REST responses. Two transports reach one runtime, so concealing only the route left the same disclosure available. Recorded separately because it shows the cost of repairing a route rather than a rule. After the binding fix the cross-tenant path no longer reaches the handler at all, so what remains reachable is a caller naming a sibling client inside their own project; that is the path the test exercises.

findings.title: GET /status reported a platform-wide Studio session count
findings.notes: Every other field in the response was filtered to the caller's authorized clients, while sessionCount came from an unfiltered platform-wide listing. The session listing route already did the correct filtering, so the fix reuses it rather than introducing a rule. Low severity on its own: it exposes a count, not identities or content.

findings.title: The shared project access control distinguishes another tenant's project from one that does not exist
findings.notes: requireProjectAccess answers 404 Project not found for an unknown id and 403 Access denied for a project that exists and belongs to someone else, so any caller can enumerate which project ids are real. Confirmed behaviourally: the same request pair returned 403 and 404 respectively. This is the disclosure closed for Studio commands and Studio clients, one level down, in the control every project-scoped route depends on. Deliberately not fixed alongside the Studio work: hasProjectAccess already returns a bare boolean and is what concealing callers use, so the repair belongs to the canonical MAR-001 helper rather than to another route. Changing requireProjectAccess in isolation would also alter responses across every route that uses it, which needs its own slice and its own evidence. Fixed through the canonical helper rather than in place. requireProjectAccess now resolves the project through requireOwned, so a project that exists and is not the caller's and one that does not exist produce the same status and the same body. Baseline reproduced before the change: the same request pair returned 403 and 404. Authentication is unaffected, because an absent caller is not a concealed resource: an unauthenticated request still answers 401. Three existing tests pinned the disclosing behaviour and were updated to assert the stronger property instead, including one written during the blueprint slice whose purpose was to guard that this control had not changed.

findings.title: Route-level authorization had no canonical mechanism, so each route decided separately what to authorize and what to disclose
findings.notes: Four Studio findings shared one shape: the identifier the caller was authorized for was not the thing the operation acted on. requireOwned takes the resource's own id and a loader, and derives the authoritative project from what the loader returned. It has no parameter for a caller-supplied project, so the mismatch is unrepresentable rather than discouraged; a helper that accepted a project alongside a resource id would be a tidier spelling of the same defect. denyAsAbsent builds the refusal from the resource name rather than the resource, so a denial has nothing of the refused object in it to leak. filterOwned was designed and deliberately not built: this slice has no list endpoint to migrate, and the existing per-route filters already work. Only SEC-PROJECT-ACCESS-DISCLOSURE-001 is migrated here; the remaining 93 unreviewed bindings are later slices.

findings.title: Refusing another tenant's conversation disclosed that the conversation existed
findings.notes: The conversation routes resolved correctly and no caller could read or delete another tenant's conversation, but a missing conversation answered 'Conversation not found' while another tenant's answered 'Project not found', so the two bodies revealed which conversation ids were real. Reproduced against the baseline before the change. Migrated to requireOwned, which loads the conversation, derives the project from it and answers both through denyAsAbsent. POST /message carries a conversationId and a projectId together, the shape that produced SEC-STUDIO-PROTOCOL-BINDING-001; here the service already ignored the body projectId whenever a conversation was named, and a test now pins that rather than trusting it.

findings.title: The canonical helper depended on an access-control method the interface marked optional
findings.notes: Found while migrating the conversation routes, not by review. hasProjectAccess is optional on ProjectAccessControl, and requireOwned failed closed when it was absent, so a route wired to a control that omitted it refused every request as absent. An existing durability test caught it, which is the only reason it did not reach production as a silent outage. The helper now takes the check as a required argument rather than reaching into an access control for it, and ProjectRuntime declares that what it hands out provides it, so the situation cannot be constructed at a migration site.

findings.title: Refusing another tenant's execution job disclosed that the job existed
findings.notes: The job routes loaded the job and authorized the job's own project, so no caller could read or retry another tenant's. A job that did not exist answered 'Job not found' while another tenant's fell through to the project control and answered 'Project not found', so the pair revealed which job ids were real. Reproduced against the baseline. It mattered most beside POST /retry, which re-queues work and therefore spends compute; the regression test asserts the refused job stays in the dead-letter queue rather than only checking the status.

findings.title: The job status route answered a second time after the access check had already refused
findings.notes: GET /job/:id wrote its own 404 after requireJobProjectAccess had already answered, so every denied request threw ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT. The refusal reached the caller intact, but on the server it surfaced as an unhandled rejection rather than as a refusal, which turns a routine denial into log noise that hides real faults. Pre-existing, not introduced by the migration: the same errors appear in the baseline run. The first attempt to pin it listened for uncaughtException and passed with the defect restored; it catches the fault only as an unhandled rejection, which is what the test now asserts.

findings.title: Plan access was correct and unexercised
findings.notes: The plan routes derive the project from the stored plan, conceal a foreign plan as an absent one, and authorize before POST /execute runs any agent. Execution options take the project from plan.goal.projectId rather than from the request. Recorded as a verified control rather than migrated: rewriting a correct check to resemble the others would carry a migration's risk for no change in behaviour. What it lacked was evidence, which it now has.

findings.title: Regenerating the authorization matrix discarded every recorded cross-tenant verdict
findings.notes: The matrix is generated, and four remediation slices recorded their evidence by editing the generated file. Running the generator reset 27 operations to indirect-unreviewed and none-recorded, and nothing failed: no check compared the committed matrix against what the generator produces. Found by running the generator during this closure, not by review. Verdicts now live in the generator's binding rules so regeneration reproduces them, and a --check mode wired into npm run validate refuses a committed matrix the generator would not produce. Proved both ways: a hand edit exits 1, a regenerated file exits 0.

findings.title: MAR-001 has fifteen operations left where nothing canonical protects the resource
findings.notes: Four families, none of which the canonical helper covers as it stands. (1) concept.ts session-owned-concept, 3 operations: ownership is a Map from concept id to user id, so the parent is a user rather than a project and requireOwned, which is project-derived, does not apply. (2) body-blueprint-project, 8 operations across economy, generation-v2, lifecycle, simulation and world: a blueprint identifier taken from the body is passed to requireProjectAccess as though it were a project identifier, which is AUDIT-BODY-SUPPLIED-BLUEPRINT-001. (3) socket project:join and project:leave, which is AUDIT-REALTIME-ROOM-001. (4) api/v1 plan routes, 2 operations: a second plan surface beside routes/planning.ts, unexercised, and duplication is the reason it was missed. Memory operations are deliberately not here: they classify as direct-project, and isolating what memory holds belongs to MAR-008 rather than to resource binding.

findings.title: Autonomous session control was correct and unexercised
findings.notes: Two helpers, both concealing: one resolves the session and derives its project, the other takes a project directly, and each answers 'Session not found' for an absent session and for another tenant's alike. Four operations mutate a running session, so the tests assert the session never entered a state only pause, resume, cancel or recover can produce, rather than comparing a status captured before the calls — the orchestrator finishes the run on its own and that comparison raced it. Recorded as a verified control, not migrated: no production code was changed. Sensitivity proved by neutralising each helper in turn; the first attempt only neutralised one and left the read assertions passing, which is how the second helper was found.

findings.title: The plugin destroyed and overwrote creator-authored scripts without checking ownership
findings.notes: ArtifactLoader:_upsertScript took whatever instance already carried the target name. On a class mismatch it destroyed it; otherwise it overwrote Source. Neither branch asked whether the instance was the plugin's own, and scripts the plugin created were never marked AIStudioManaged, so the ownership machinery the UI and world materializers rely on could not see them either. A creator's hand-written module sitting where generated output wanted to be was deleted without a word. Reproduced against the baseline by running the plugin's own Lua: the creator's ModuleScript came back destroyed and the creator's Source came back replaced. A collision with unmarked work is now refused, the plugin's own output stays freely replaceable, and created scripts are marked.

findings.title: An unrecognised script root fell back to the container that replicates to every client
findings.notes: _resolveRoot returned ReplicatedStorage with the unrecognised segment demoted to a folder name, so a typo or a root this plugin version had not heard of landed silently in a replicated container. A server Script placed there does not run, but its source replicates to every client, so a placement mistake became a disclosure of server logic. Nothing checked class against container either, so ReplicatedStorage/Secret.server.lua was accepted outright. Both reproduced against the baseline. An unnameable destination is now refused, and a class may only occupy a container that can run it.

findings.title: The Studio plugin had no executable test path
findings.notes: Every claim about the plugin was a string search over its source, which cannot show that a creator's script survived a generation or that a bad root was refused. That is the same weak evidence MAR-001 spent four slices replacing, and it would have made every MAR-002 fix unprovable. A Lua runtime was added as a dev dependency and a Roblox instance stub written for it, so the plugin's own modules run and their effects are observed. The stub models Parent reassignment, Destroy, attributes and IsA, and raises on any class or service it does not model, because a stub that quietly returns nil turns a real defect into a passing test.

findings.title: The materializer sweep removes any managed instance, including another project's
findings.notes: isManaged reads one boolean attribute, which answers whether AI Studio made the instance and not whether this project did. The sweep removes every managed child the current delivery did not name, so a place file that has hosted two projects loses the first project's screens to the second project's export. Reproduced: a screen created by one delivery is destroyed by the next. The replace path is NOT affected and is deliberately untouched here, because it already runs an ownership precheck before constructing anything and refuses a collision with unmanaged work. Not fixed in this pass: materialize(content, stageFolder) receives no project identity, so the correct behaviour is not merely unenforced but unrepresentable. The contract has to change first, which is SEC-STUDIO-PROVENANCE-CONTRACT-001. Fixed. materialize now takes a project and delivery, stamps both on every instance it creates, and gates replace and sweep on a matching project; the loader carries the pair. An instance with the mark and no project is treated as foreign, with no migration and no heuristic attribution, because guessing in the permissive direction is the finding. The baseline file that recorded the defect was removed rather than inverted: its two defect assertions no longer describe anything, and its other assertions are covered by the contract file.

findings.title: The materializer contract carries no project identity to scope ownership against
findings.notes: UITreeMaterializer.materialize and WorldSceneMaterializer.materialize take content and a stage folder. Neither the arguments nor the content carry a project, and the loader that calls them does not pass one, so no destructive decision can be scoped to the delivery it belongs to. Smallest contract that closes it: stamp two attributes beside AIStudioManaged when an instance is created, one naming the project and one naming the delivery that produced it, and pass the expected pair into materialize. Replace and sweep then require managed AND a matching project, treating a managed instance from elsewhere exactly as they already treat unmanaged work: refuse rather than destroy. An instance carrying the mark but no project attribute is from a build before this change and must be treated as foreign, because guessing in the permissive direction is what the finding is about. Fixed. materialize now takes a project and delivery, stamps both on every instance it creates, and gates replace and sweep on a matching project; the loader carries the pair. An instance with the mark and no project is treated as foreign, with no migration and no heuristic attribution, because guessing in the permissive direction is the finding. The baseline file that recorded the defect was removed rather than inverted: its two defect assertions no longer describe anything, and its other assertions are covered by the contract file.

findings.title: Lua runtime added as a development dependency for Studio plugin tests
findings.notes: wasmoon@1.16.0, reviewed as a devDependency for a public repository. Verdict SAFE_WITH_CONDITIONS, no blocker. No advisories in OSV, GHSA or the npm bulk endpoint for this version; no malware signal; valid registry signature; MIT; no install scripts, with the WASM binary shipped pre-built inside the tarball rather than fetched at install time. Its real transitive footprint is one types-only package. Condition: 1.16.0 dates from December 2023 with no later 1.x release and development moved to a 2.0 prerelease, so the caret range will not pick up a patch that does not exist and the version needs checking by hand rather than assumed current. Review gaps recorded rather than glossed: no Endor data was available, no dedicated malware feed was queried, the bundled binary was not diffed against a reproducible build, and the maintainer account's 2FA posture could not be verified.

findings.title: Scripts and metadata values were owned by AI Studio but not by any project
findings.notes: The materializers were given a project and delivery, but the two instance kinds the loader writes itself, scripts and the metadata StringValue, still decided ownership from the managed mark alone. The boundary therefore held for a generated screen and not for the script beside it, and the weaker half decides the boundary. Both now stamp the same three attributes and gate replacement on a matching project, with an unattributed managed instance treated as foreign exactly as elsewhere. Reproduced against the baseline: eight assertions failed before the change, including a script and a metadata value belonging to another project being silently overwritten. Reverse-proved separately for stamping, for the ownership check and for the missing-provenance guard; each revert fails a distinct set. A stub gap surfaced during the baseline rather than being papered over: HttpService had no JSONEncode, and the stub raised instead of returning nil, which is why it was noticed.

findings.title: Provenance was enforced but never set, and would have been plugin-global if it had been
findings.notes: setProvenance had no caller anywhere in the plugin, so in a real session every import would have been refused by the rule meant to protect it: correct and unreachable, which is worse than either alone. It was also the wrong shape. One ArtifactLoader serves the whole plugin session, so identity stored on it outlives the import that set it; a later call that forgot would write under whichever project went last, and an import interleaved across the HTTP yields inside a poll could write under the other. Rather than clearing the field, the field was removed: provenance is passed per loadArtifact call and is import-scoped by construction, so there is no stale state to clear and no window to race. SyncManager derives it from the queued EXPORT_PROJECT payload, which the backend authorized and which is validated for a non-empty project and execution before anything is written, rather than from the connector's own project. Reverse-proved twice: dropping the argument fails three assertions, and sourcing the project from the connector instead of the payload fails two.

findings.title: Studio creator-ownership boundary closed locally across every path that writes
findings.notes: Every path the plugin writes through now stamps a project and a delivery and refuses to replace or sweep anything it cannot prove is this project's: scripts, metadata values, UI screens and world zones. Hand-built work, another project's work and work carrying the mark with no project all get the same refusal. Identity comes from the backend-authorized export command and travels per call, so there is no shared mutable state to go stale between imports. The world path was fixed alongside the UI one but only the UI one had been exercised; it now has its own sweep and replace tests, because fixing two things and proving one is how a regression ships in the half nobody looked at. Idempotence holds and is now evidenced in both directions: a command the backend verified is not applied twice, and one it never confirmed is retried, which is why the guard sits after verification rather than before it. Concurrency is deliberately excluded. Import-scoped provenance removed the mutable state a cross-project race needed, which is a design property rather than a measurement; real interleaving belongs to MAR-016. Remaining MAR-002 surface is Studio session and command lifecycle rather than creator ownership.

findings.title: A start request whose response was lost could not be retried safely
findings.notes: Single-flight was already durable, so the gap was request identity rather than admission. A start that succeeded on the server and whose response never reached the caller is indistinguishable from one that never arrived, and repeating it produced one of two wrong answers. Reproduced against the baseline: while the run was active the retry got ActiveGenerationConflictError naming an execution the caller could not identify as its own, and once the run had finished and released its claim the same retry silently started a second generation, incrementing the count and spending provider budget again. A durable record keyed by project and idempotency key is now committed in the same applyDurableBatch as the start evidence and the claim, so a repeat returns the original execution without preparing, enqueueing or counting anything. The same key with a different principal or payload is refused rather than answered, because two requests claiming one identity cannot be resolved by guessing. The coordinator does not fabricate the caller's result on a replay; the caller supplies a resolver, since nothing was prepared. Reverse-proved separately for the replay, for the conflict check and for committing the record inside the transaction rather than beside it. No crash window remains between the record, the claim, the execution and the history: they are one batch whose contract is that a rejection preserves the exact pre-transaction state. Integrated into the request path in a follow-up commit on the same branch. The key arrives as a required `Idempotency-Key` request header rather than a server-generated value, because the server cannot mint a value that names 'the same request' before the request exists, and minting one on a miss would make every retry look like a fresh request. Required rather than optional: an optional key leaves the same hole open for whichever caller forgets one, so a missing header is a 400 answered before any blueprint lookup or durable work. It is bound to the principal, the project, and a fingerprint of the one body field that changes what gets generated. Two conflict shapes are distinguished on the wire by a `code` field, because 'someone else is already generating' and 'you reused a key for a different request' need different client responses. Reverse-proved at the route level in four separate reverts: removing the required-header check fails only the missing-key case, collapsing the fingerprint fails only the changed-payload case, restoring per-project key scoping fails only the two cross-project cases, and unwiring the request object entirely fails all four replay and conflict cases.

findings.title: An idempotency key partitioned per project could not detect its own reuse across projects
findings.notes: The first implementation keyed the durable record by `${projectId}:${key}`. A key is supposed to name one logical request, so the same key surfacing against a different project has to fail closed as a caller defect. Partitioning by project made that collision structurally undetectable: the two requests would never read the same record, and each project would quietly get its own start under a key that was meant to be unique. Found while writing the route contract rather than by review, because the invariant 'same key + different project => conflict' had no test until the HTTP contract was pinned. The record is now keyed by the key alone with the project stored as a checked field. Reverse-proved by restoring the per-project id, which fails exactly the two cross-project tests and nothing else.
